title: POC weekly sync - throughput optimization
summary: Weekly POC check-in to review throughput numbers from the latest run, discuss tweaks to continuous batching and concurrency targets, and agree next steps for a 24h production-like benchmark. Customer still evaluating Dedicated vs Hosted and concerned about VPC routing, encryption, and predictable latency under burst traffic.
topics: Continuous batching parameter tuning & target concurrency
Security / VPC peering and KMS concerns
Next steps: 24h run, config handoff, demo for infra team
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-11-25 15:00 PST | Duration: ~45m | Attendees: Jason Miller (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Michael Chen (Atlas Eng Lead), Laura Gomez (ML), Samir Patel (Platform)

[00:00] Jason Miller: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick check, can you hear us ok?
[00:07] Michael Chen: Yep, good here. Thanks Jason.
[00:12] Priya Shah: Great, I'll jump straight into the numbers we ran over the weekend, we've got the aggregated throughput spreadsheets linked in the notes - throughput-benchmarks.xlsx - but I put the headline: sustained 2.6k tokens/sec at p95 latency of 240ms on the ded-8xA100 config with continuous batching at batch_window=40ms.
[00:35] Laura Gomez: Sorry can you repeat p95 number? The line dropped a bit for me.
[00:40] Priya Shah: p95 about two hundred and forty ms, p50 around 85ms. There is some variation when we hit concurrency above 160, that's where you see queue growth.
[00:52] Samir Patel: When you say concurrency 160, that's concurrent requests or inflight tokens?
[00:57] Priya Shah: concurrent requests. We triggered concurrency via our load tool to simulate your predicted burst profile.
[01:05] Jason Miller: To add, we saw continuous batching help a lot for median — the big wins are at moderate concurrency where batches get to 8-12 sequences. At very high concurrency you hit limits on the runtime's kernel scheduling, and your latency profile shifts.
[01:22] Michael Chen: Right, that matches what we saw in our internal runs. Our question is can we push more tokens/sec by changing concurrency targets vs increasing batch_window? Which is less risky for tail latency?
[01:34] Priya Shah: Good question. Increasing batch_window (say from 40ms to 80ms) increases batching efficiency and pushes tokens/sec up but adds extra latency to some requests. The knob we recommend is to set a dynamic concurrency target: keep per-worker concurrency low (like 8) and increase global concurrency but with a queue depth cap and backpressure.
[01:52] Laura Gomez: We noticed the queue depth cap in the config had default 500, we reduced to 200 — that dropped p95 but reduced throughput. There was some mis-configuration earlier where the KV cash was off, so prefix caching wasn't kicking in for a subset of traffic.
[02:08] Priya Shah: Yeah, there was a misspelling in our runbook earlier — KV cache, sorry, I said cash then. The prefix cache hits were only ~18% for that dataset; when we enabled prefix caching properly it went up to ~65% and tokens/sec improved by ~20%.
[02:26] Michael Chen: That seems promising. Can you share the exact config we should apply?
[02:30] Jason Miller: We'll drop the tuned config in the shared folder — redwood-configs/atlas-throughput-20261125.yaml and include comments for batch_window, max_inflight_per_worker, and queue_depth.
[02:40] Samir Patel: On the infra side, we need to understand the Dedicated sizing. If we use Dedicated we want predictable p95 under 250ms for our SLA, even during peak market open. If Hosted we may see more variability.
[02:54] Priya Shah: Dedicated buys isolation and more predictable kernels, yes. We can also pin model variants and enable fallback to a slightly quantized variant on overflow. That buys capacity but may affect semantic fidelity.
[03:08] Laura Gomez: Did you run quantized model variants in the weekend runs?
[03:11] Priya Shah: We ran q4_0 and q5_0 variants; q5_0 was close in quality and saved about 30% tokens/sec cost, q4_0 gave more throughput but with some drop in long-form coherency on our eval prompts.
[03:26] Michael Chen: Quality regression is a big deal for compliance — we have to show QA that answers meet our regulatory script.
[03:31] Jason Miller: Totally, that's why our recommendation is to use A/B rollout and do canary for quantized variants with your eval set. Redwood Optimize can tie the regression alerts to your prompt set and auto-rollback if quality dips.
[03:46] Samir Patel: Two quick infra items — VPC peering latency to Redwood region, and KMS integration. We can't have keys leaving our KMS.
[03:54] Priya Shah: For Private we support customer-managed KMS and HSM integration; for Hosted we offer envelope encryption with BYOK but keys do transit to our control plane for management unless you choose Private. We'll share the security pack (security-pack.pdf) with exact flow diagrams.
[04:12] Michael Chen: Good. Back to throughput: you mentioned dynamic concurrency and per-worker inflight limits. Can you explain how we set the global target?
[04:20] Priya Shah: Sure. Global target = number_workers * target_inflight_per_worker * average_tokens_in_flight. But practically we target a concurrency region — e.g., start at global 120, monitor queue growth and adjust using autoscaler rules. You can set a soft cap so requests get queued until queue depth threshold then start rejecting with 503 or fallback to a smaller model.
[04:42] Laura Gomez: Are we able to test the fallback model in this PoC? We want to see behavioral degradation metrics.
[04:48] Jason Miller: Yes, we can add a fallback policy in the next run. We'll set a fallback to q5_0 after queue depth > 250 or p95 > 300ms for 60s. That gives you seamless degradation.
[05:03] [Break — load generator params discussion, timestamps omitted]
[08:00] Priya Shah: Ok quick recap of what we changed this week for the run: enable prefix caching fix, increase batch_window from 30->40ms, set per-worker inflight=8, global concurrency target=150, queue_depth cap=200, fallback policy to q5_0 launched at thresholds. That produced the weekend numbers.
[08:25] Michael Chen: Can you call out the specific throughput numbers again? I want them in the notes.
[08:30] Priya Shah: Sure. Sustained tokens/sec 2600, peak tokens/sec short bursts ~3200, p50 85ms, p95 240ms, error rate 0.02% (timeouts at very high bursts).
[08:44] Laura Gomez: The error pattern we saw was timeouts clustered when concurrency ramped quickly — looks like load generator was more aggressive than our expected traffic shape.
[08:53] Priya Shah: Right — smoothing the arrival rate (introducing a small ramp) reduced the queue spikes. We recommended a leaky-bucket throttler on your gateway to match production arrival shapes.
[09:05] Samir Patel: About the 24h run — what should we expect to see versus the short weekend run?
[09:10] Jason Miller: Longer run surfaces memory leaks, stateful cache patterns, and kernel scheduling jitter. We'll run full 24h with production-like ARR (arrival patterns), mixed prompt lengths, and a few long-context sessions to see KV cache behavior.
[09:26] Michael Chen: How long do you think the config tuning will take after we do 24h?
[09:30] Priya Shah: Typically 3-5 days to iterate on config+autoscaler policies, shorter if metrics look stable. We'll provide a checklist for gating the pilot to Prod.
[09:38] Laura Gomez: One more question—how do we validate semantic quality while doing throughput optimization? We don't want throughput wins at the cost of hallucination.
[09:46] Jason Miller: You'll need a small eval set of representative prompts; Redwood Optimize attaches regression alerts to that set. We'll help instrument the eval hooks during the 24h run and set alert thresholds.
[10:00] Michael Chen: Any competitors coming up for consideration? We compared notes earlier with some managed endpoints; latency was better elsewhere on p50 but cost was higher.
[10:09] Priya Shah: They mentioned Anthropic and in-house on GKE. Competitors_mentioned in notes are Anthropic and in-house GKE endpoints.
[10:17] Jason Miller: Ok let's go over next steps and action items
[10:20] Priya Shah: Action item: Jason to share redwood-configs/atlas-throughput-20261125.yaml and throughput-benchmarks.xlsx.
[10:27] Jason Miller: I'll also open a ticket with Support to schedule the 24h run on your Dedicated stack next Friday (2026-12-03) — pending your infra signoff.
[10:36] Michael Chen: We need the security diagrams and KMS flow before we greenlight Dedicated.
[10:41] Jason Miller: We'll send security-pack.pdf and a short SSO/SAML checklist.
[10:46] Laura Gomez: We'll run our internal acceptance tests against the tuned config and report any functional regressions.
[10:50] Samir Patel: Please include the autoscaler rules you recommend for peak market open to avoid sudden pre-emption.
[10:56] Priya Shah: Sure — we'll include autoscaler policy examples and an example HPA-style config for Dedicated.
[11:03] Jason Miller: Great. Any other questions?
[11:06] Michael Chen: Not for now. Thanks everyone.
[11:09] Jason Miller: Thanks, we'll send notes and configs by EOD and schedule the 24h run once infra is cleared.
[11:15] End of meeting

Apply prefix caching fix and re-run short test to validate cache hit rate >60%
